sentences.text: It explained with the particular patience of somebody who has explained the same thing many times and has stopped being irritated by it, which Marisol thought was probably a considerable achievement.
Most mapmakers, it said, draw what is there.
This is useful.
Nobody is saying it is not useful.
If you want to know where the stream is, a map of where the stream is will tell you where the stream is, and you can go and put your hand in it and confirm the matter.
But it is not interesting.

"I draw," said the hare, "what is going to be there." Marisol asked how that was possible, which she was slightly ashamed of afterwards, because it was the obvious question and the hare had clearly been asked it a great many times.
The answer was not what she expected.
"Paths are not built," it said.
"Almost nobody understands this.
People think somebody decides — a council, a landowner, somebody with a plan — and then men come with gravel.
That is a road.
A road is built.
A path is worn." It got down off the stack of paper it had been sitting on and went to the wall of the office, where a larger map was pinned up with thorns.
"Somebody goes first," it said.
"One person.
And they go through the wrong part of the bracken, at the wrong time of year, usually for a bad reason.
They have left something at the top.
They are avoiding somebody on the road.
They are twelve and they are in a temper.
The reason is nearly always small and nearly always private." "And then?" "And then the bracken is bent.
Only a little.

But the next person who comes along that way — and there is always a next person, that is the whole trick of it — the next person finds that going where the bracken is bent is very slightly easier than going where it is not.
And they are not deciding anything.
They are not thinking about it at all.
They are simply taking the easier of two options, which is what everything alive does, always." It turned round.
"Do that four hundred times and you have a path.
Do it four thousand times and somebody puts up a sign with the mileage on it and a little picture of a boot.
And by then everyone has completely forgotten that there was a first person, and that the first person went that way by mistake." Marisol sat back on her heels.
"So how do you know which way the first person will go?" There was a pause.
"I don't," said the hare.
"I guess." "You guess?" "I guess extremely well.
I have been doing it for a long time and I understand where people are likely to leave a jumper.
But it is a guess, and I have been wrong four hundred and six times, and I do not enjoy discussing it."
